big: Think of a portfolio like a house with a solid foundation and a few rooms you keep redecorating. The foundation is the core. The rooms are satellites. The art is in keeping the rooms small.

lines: My cousin made 60% on a defence fund last year. I want to put half my savings in it.
I understand the pull. Let us split your money in two jobs: a core that compounds quietly, and a small satellite for bets like that one.

alt: Three bars: the start, after the satellite doubles, and after trimming back to 30 percent
caps: Start with ₹10 lakh: core 75% (flexi cap, index, multi-asset) and satellite 25% (defence, small cap, silver).
The satellite doubles to ₹5 lakh while the core stands still. Now the portfolio is ₹12.5 lakh.
Satellite is now 40%. It was meant to be a small bet and has become the main one.
Trim ₹1.25 lakh back to the core. Satellite returns to 30%, the cap.

alt: Two bars comparing the satellite share and the loss when the satellite halves, with and without trimming
caps: Now the satellite turns. Compare a portfolio left to run with one trimmed to 30%.
Left to run, the satellite is 40%, or ₹5 lakh. Trimmed, it is 30%, or ₹3.75 lakh.
Satellite halves. Left to run, the portfolio loses ₹2.5 lakh, 20%. Trimmed, it loses about ₹1.9 lakh, 15%.
Same bet, same fall. A smaller satellite hurts less.

alt: Three lines: core alone, satellite alone, and a blend trimmed to a 30 percent satellite over ten made-up years
caps: Made-up decade, not real data. The core grows steadily and never falls more than about 5%.
The satellite alone swings wildly: it ends highest, but it drops about 45% along the way.
The blend: 75% core, 25% satellite, trimmed whenever the satellite passes 30%.
It ends ahead of the core (₹250 against ₹218) with a fall of about 16%, far less than the satellite's.

q: A ₹10 lakh portfolio is 75% core and 25% satellite. The satellite doubles and the core is unchanged. With a 30% cap on satellites, what should the investor do?
opts: Do nothing, because a doubled satellite is a sign that it should be given more room
Move about ₹1.25 lakh from the satellite to the core, since it is 40% of ₹12.5 lakh
Move ₹2.5 lakh from the satellite to the core, so it returns to its original 25% weight
Sell the whole satellite, because a bet that doubles may fall back at any time
why: Letting satellites grow past the cap is how a small bet turns into the main risk of the portfolio.
Satellite is ₹5 lakh of ₹12.5 lakh, 40%. The cap of 30% is ₹3.75 lakh, so ₹1.25 lakh goes back to the core.
The cap is 30%, not the old 25%. Moving ₹2.5 lakh would be a bigger trade than the rule needs.
Selling all of it discards the very purpose of a satellite, a limited shot at extra growth.

q: A client wants to put a defence fund into her core because it returned 60% last year. Where does the adviser place it, and why?
opts: In the satellite: a theme is a conviction bet, and the core holds broad funds
In the core, because a 60% return shows it has earned a place among the stable funds
In neither, because a thematic fund is not allowed inside any sort of portfolio
In the core, as long as it is bought in a single lump sum rather than as a SIP
why: Core means flexi cap, index and multi-asset funds that compound steadily. Defence is a narrow theme, so it sits in the satellite.
One good year is a weak reason. A narrow theme can swing hard, which is what a core is meant to avoid.
Thematic funds are allowed. They are best held in a limited satellite, not banned from the portfolio.
The way of buying does not change the fund's character. A defence theme stays a satellite either way.

q: After a rally, a client's satellite funds make up 45% of his portfolio. Which plan fits the core-and-satellite approach?
opts: Let the winners run, since a satellite that grows has clearly proved its worth
Sell the core to buy more satellites, because that is where the returns have come from
Switch every satellite into a single fund so that the weight looks smaller on paper
Trim satellites to the 20% to 30% band, add to the core, and check tax first
why: A rally does not prove the future. Past gains swell the weight, and a fall then hurts a large satellite more.
Shrinking the core to chase the winner reverses the design. The core is the foundation to be kept.
Merging satellites into one fund does not change how much money is exposed to risky bets.
The core stays; the satellites flex. Trimming to the band keeps conviction bets small. Sales can carry tax.

q: A portfolio is 60% core. The satellite is defence 15%, small cap 15% and silver 10%. The cap is 30% for the satellite sleeve. What follows?
opts: Nothing, because each satellite fund is under 30% and the cap applies per fund
Trim the core instead, since it has the largest weight in the whole portfolio
Satellites total 40%, over the cap, so trim satellites rather than the core
Nothing, because splitting the satellite across three funds spreads the risk away
why: The cap is for the whole sleeve. Three funds that each look small can still add up to a large bet.
The core is meant to be the stable base. Trimming it enlarges the risky part instead of cutting it.
The cap applies to the satellite sleeve as a whole: 15 plus 15 plus 10 is 40%. Trimming brings it back to 30%.
Spreading across themes helps a little, but all three are conviction bets and still total 40%.

pts: Core (70% to 80%): flexi cap, index, multi-asset, for steady compounding. Satellite (20% to 30%): defence, small cap, silver, for conviction bets.
Satellites flex or switch; the core stays. After a rally, trim satellites back to the cap and add to the core.
The cap applies to the sleeve as a whole. A satellite at 40% turns a small bet into the main risk.
